Scotland: A Motorcyclist's Paradise

Scotland offers some of the most spectacular motorcycle riding in Europe. From the sweeping Highland passes to the dramatic coastal roads of the west, every mile delivers jaw-dropping scenery and rewarding tarmac. Whether you're chasing single-track adventures or flowing A-road sweepers, Scotland has it all.

1. The A82 Through Glen Coe

Often cited as Britain's most dramatic road, the A82 through Glen Coe is a must-ride for any motorcyclist visiting Scotland. The road winds through a glacial valley flanked by towering peaks, with the Three Sisters looming overhead. Start from Tyndrum and ride north — the views only get better. Watch for slow-moving campervans in summer and always keep an eye on the weather, as conditions can change rapidly.

2. Bealach na Bà (Applecross)

The Bealach na Bà is Britain's answer to an Alpine pass. Rising to 626 metres with gradients up to 20%, this single-track road features tight hairpin bends and sheer drops. The descent towards Applecross village rewards you with stunning views over Skye and Raasay. Ride it early morning to avoid tourist traffic.

3. The A87 to Skye

The A87 from Invergarry to the Skye Bridge is one of Scotland's finest touring roads. It passes through Glen Shiel, where the Five Sisters of Kintail rise dramatically on either side. The road surface is generally excellent and the sweeping bends make for satisfying progress.

Pro tip: Fill up at Invergarry or Dornie — fuel stations are sparse on the way to Skye.

4. The A838 and A894 — Far North

The far north of Scotland is gloriously empty. The A838 from Durness to Lairg and the A894 past Kylesku Bridge offer remote, traffic-free riding through some of Europe's last true wilderness. Single-track sections add to the adventure. The Kylesku Bridge itself is a stunning curved structure spanning a sea loch.

5-8. More Essential Scottish Roads

  • A9 Inverness to Caithness — Fast dual carriageway sections with vast Highland panoramas
  • A835 Ullapool Road — Sweeping bends past Loch Glascarnoch with mountain backdrops
  • A93 Cairngorm Pass — The highest public road in Britain at 665m, superb in autumn colours
  • B8007 to Ardnamurchan — Remote peninsula road to Britain's most westerly point

Planning Your Scottish Motorcycle Trip

Scotland's roads are best enjoyed between May and September, though midges can be fierce from June to August. Always carry waterproofs — rain can arrive without warning. The west coast sees more rainfall than the east, but the scenery more than compensates.

Fuel and Facilities

In the Highlands, fuel stations can be 50+ miles apart. Never pass a fuel station below half tank. Many rural stations close at 6pm and some don't open on Sundays. Carry a tyre repair kit and basic tools, as mobile signal is patchy in remote areas. Accommodation books up fast in summer — consider wild camping, which is legal in Scotland under the right to roam.

Road Conditions

Scottish B-roads can have loose gravel, potholes, and single-track sections with passing places. Ride within your limits, especially on unfamiliar roads. Livestock (sheep, deer, Highland cattle) can appear without warning. Despite these challenges, Scotland remains the UK's ultimate motorcycling destination. The far north A838 and A894 past Kylesku Bridge offer near traffic-free wilderness riding on part-single-track roads.
Best ridden May to September, but midges are fierce from June to August and the west coast catches far more rain.

faq.q: When is the best time to ride in Scotland?
faq.a: May to September offers the longest days and most settled weather, though nowhere in the Highlands is ever guaranteed dry. Midges are at their worst from June to August, so many riders favour May and September for a good balance of daylight, quieter roads and fewer biting insects.

faq.q: How far apart are fuel stations in the Highlands?
faq.a: In remote areas fuel stations can be more than 50 miles apart, many close at 6pm and some do not open on Sundays. Fill up at Invergarry or Dornie before heading to Skye, and never pass a station below half a tank on the west coast.

faq.q: Is the Bealach na Ba suitable for beginners?
faq.a: It is challenging rather than dangerous. The single-track climb rises to 626 metres with gradients up to 20% and tight hairpins, so confident clutch control and hill-start ability help. Ride it early morning to avoid tourist traffic and take passing places on your left calmly.

faq.q: What hazards should I expect on Scottish B-roads?
faq.a: Expect loose gravel, potholes and single-track sections with passing places. Sheep, deer and Highland cattle can appear without warning, and mobile signal is patchy. Carry a tyre repair kit and basic tools, and ride well within your limits on unfamiliar roads.
